title: Rav Kook
hookLine: a mystic chief rabbi who saw holiness in secular pioneers

lines: A RABBI WHO WRITES MYSTICAL POETRY.
cards: On a Friday evening, young pioneers finish work late in the fields. No candles, no kiddush, no synagogue; some of them left religion behind on purpose.

Down the road lives a rabbi who keeps the commandments with great care and writes mystical poetry. A rabbi like that might be expected to scold them. Instead he speaks of them with something close to love.
Their sweat in the soil, he says, is holy work, even if they would never use that word. His name is Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, known as Rav Kook.

teach.b: Rav Kook came to the land of Israel as the rabbi of the port city of Jaffa, and later became chief rabbi under British rule. He was a legal scholar, and also a mystic, and his mysticism drew on an old Kabbalah teaching.
When the world was made, it says, sparks of divine light scattered and fell into everything, even into places that look empty of God. A person's work is to find those sparks and lift them up.
Rav Kook looked at the secular pioneers, the labor Zionists, the kibbutz builders, and said: there are sparks in this too.
Their longing for justice, their love of the land, their willingness to give up comfort for their people. To him these were holy, even when the people carrying them denied any holiness at all.
A saying often linked to him sums up his hope: the old will be made new, and the new will be made holy.
Not everyone was happy with this. Some rabbis thought he was far too generous to people who broke the Sabbath. Some pioneers did not want to be told their work was secretly religious.
Rav Kook kept to his view. A line in Genesis fits him.
Jacob wakes from his dream of the ladder and says, "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." Rav Kook looked at people who did not know, and believed it anyway.

how: Rav Kook's writings are studied in religious Zionist yeshivas and beyond, and his teaching that holiness can be found in secular life is quoted well beyond those circles, while others disagree with it.

games.q: you are Rav Kook. young pioneers near you work on Shabbat and laugh at religion. what do you say about them?
o: they are lost to their people.
their work holds sparks of holiness.
games.why: he saw their longing for justice and love of the land as holy, even when they denied it.

practice: Think of someone you don't naturally admire, maybe someone who would laugh at the word holy, and look for one spark in them: a loyalty, a kindness, a stubborn honesty, a love they carry.
You don't have to approve of everything; just hold that spark in view, the way Rav Kook held the pioneers.

wordCard.voice: Rav Kook. Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, a mystic and chief rabbi who saw sparks of holiness in secular pioneers. Today's word.

orig.note: sparks: the Kabbalah word for divine light scattered into the world.

carryVoice: Your line: sparks in the secular. In Rav Kook's eyes, holiness could hide where nobody thought to look. I'll be here tomorrow.
